title: Multilevel Queue & MLFQ
summary: Partitioning processes into queues, and letting a feedback queue infer job behavior over time without ever knowing burst times in advance.

slides.markdown:
A **multilevel queue** splits processes into fixed categories (system, interactive, batch), each with its own scheduling rules. A **Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)** goes further: processes *move* between priority levels based on observed behavior, letting the scheduler approximate SJF's benefit without ever knowing burst times up front.

MLFQ is the closest thing to "how do you actually build a good general-purpose scheduler" this group covers before looking at a real production scheduler (Linux CFS) — it's the synthesis of nearly every idea from the previous three topics.

slides.sectionTitle: Multilevel queue scheduling: partitioning processes by type
slides.markdown:
A multilevel queue scheduler splits the ready queue into several permanent, separate queues by category — a common split is system processes, interactive processes, and batch processes — each with its own scheduling algorithm suited to that category (Round Robin for interactive, FCFS for batch, for example).

Queues themselves are also prioritized relative to each other: typically system > interactive > batch, meaning the scheduler only considers a lower queue when every higher queue is empty (strict priority between queues), or gives each queue a proportional CPU-time share (a fairer but more complex variant).

The key limitation, which sets up the next slide: once a process is assigned to a queue, it stays there permanently — there's no mechanism for a process to move if its actual behavior doesn't match its assigned category.

slides.sectionTitle: Limits of a static multilevel queue
slides.markdown:
A static multilevel queue has two real problems. First, misclassification: a process assigned to "batch" at creation but that later behaves interactively (or vice versa) is stuck getting the wrong treatment for its entire lifetime — the classification was a one-time guess, not an ongoing assessment.

Second, if queues are strictly prioritized (higher queue always wins), the same starvation risk from priority scheduling reappears at the queue level: if the system and interactive queues stay busy, the batch queue can starve completely, with no aging-equivalent mechanism to guarantee it eventually runs.

Both problems trace back to the same root cause: the queue assignment is fixed at creation time and never revisited based on how the process actually behaves — exactly the gap MLFQ closes.

slides.sectionTitle: Multilevel Feedback Queue: letting processes move between queues
slides.markdown:
MLFQ keeps the same idea of several priority queues, but adds the crucial fix: processes can **move between queues** based on their observed runtime behavior, not just a one-time initial assignment. All processes typically start at the highest-priority queue and get demoted or promoted as the scheduler watches how they actually behave.

This is a genuinely elegant solution to SJF's core problem (needing to know burst time in advance) — instead of predicting the future, MLFQ reacts to the past: a process that keeps using its full time slice without blocking looks CPU-bound and gets pushed down; a process that blocks quickly (for I/O) looks interactive and stays high or gets promoted.

The scheduler never needs to know burst time as a number at all — it infers "probably short/interactive" or "probably long/CPU-bound" purely from behavior it can directly observe.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: MLFQ queue structure with priority levels and quantum sizes
slides.markdown:
![Multilevel feedback queue structure](assets/mlfq-queues.svg)

Notice two design details worth naming explicitly: quantum size typically *grows* as priority drops (top queue gets short slices for fast interactive response, bottom queue gets long slices since CPU-bound jobs there don't need frequent revisits), and every process starts at the top regardless of what it turns out to be — the scheduler has to discover behavior, it can't assume it upfront.

slides.sectionTitle: The core MLFQ rules: demote CPU-bound, promote I/O-bound behavior
slides.markdown:
The classic MLFQ rule set (as formalized in the OSTEP textbook's version) boils down to a handful of rules. New processes enter at the highest-priority queue. If a process uses its entire time slice without voluntarily giving up the CPU, its priority is reduced (demoted one queue down) — a strong signal of CPU-bound behavior. If a process gives up the CPU before its slice ends (typically because it's blocking on I/O), it stays at its current priority — a signal it's likely interactive or I/O-bound, not "greedy."

The net effect after a few rounds: processes that behave like short, interactive jobs cluster near the top and get fast response times; processes that behave like long, CPU-bound jobs sink toward the bottom, where they still run (just with lower priority and longer quanta), approximating SJF-like treatment purely from observed behavior.

This is a self-correcting system: even a process misclassified initially (everyone starts at the top) gets re-classified correctly within a few scheduling rounds based on what it actually does.

slides.sectionTitle: How MLFQ approximates SJF without knowing burst times in advance
slides.markdown:
Consider two processes: a genuinely short, interactive one, and a genuinely long, CPU-bound one, both starting at the top queue. The interactive one blocks for I/O quickly and repeatedly, never using a full quantum, so it stays at high priority and keeps getting fast turns — effectively the same outcome SJF would give it, arrived at without SJF ever computing a burst-time prediction.

The CPU-bound one keeps using its full slice every time, so it demotes step by step until it settles at a low-priority queue with a long quantum — it still makes progress, just at lower priority and with less frequent interruption, roughly matching how SJF would deprioritize it relative to the short job, again without any burst-time number ever being estimated.

The insight worth internalizing: MLFQ gets SJF's *behavioral effect* — favor apparent short/interactive work — by observing history instead of predicting the future, sidestepping the exact problem that makes literal SJF impractical.

MLFQ has its own starvation risk: a process demoted to the bottom queue can get stuck there indefinitely if higher-priority interactive processes keep the top queues continuously busy — the same structural problem as static priority scheduling, just at the queue level.

The standard fix is a **periodic priority boost**: after every fixed interval (say, every 200ms of wall-clock time), move every process back to the top queue, regardless of where it currently sits. This bounds the worst-case wait for any process — it's aging's queue-level equivalent, giving the same computable guarantee that no process waits forever.

Boosting also has a second benefit beyond fairness: it lets a process whose behavior has genuinely changed (a long-running batch job that finishes its heavy computation and becomes interactive) get re-evaluated from a clean slate, rather than being permanently penalized for behavior from long ago.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a process gaming the scheduler by yielding just before quantum expiry
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The demotion rule (use your full quantum → get demoted) is a robust way to identify CPU-bound processes."

**Why it's wrong:** a naive implementation of that rule is gameable. A process can deliberately call a cheap, near-instant I/O operation (a tiny read of one byte) just before its quantum expires, technically satisfying "gave up the CPU voluntarily before the slice ended" while actually consuming almost the entire quantum's worth of real CPU work — it looks interactive to the naive rule while behaving exactly like a CPU-bound process in practice, unfairly staying at high priority.

**Correct model:** track *cumulative* CPU time used at each priority level across multiple bursts, not just whether the most recent single burst technically ended "voluntarily." A process that accumulates a full quantum's worth of CPU time across several short, sneaky bursts gets demoted just the same as one that used it in a single continuous burst — closing the gaming loophole by measuring total consumption rather than trusting the shape of individual bursts.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: MLFQ's parameters are numerous and hard to tune well
slides.markdown:
A staff-level critique of MLFQ, and part of why production kernels eventually moved away from it (see Scheduling in Practice for what Linux replaced it with): it has many independent knobs — number of queues, each queue's quantum, the demotion rule, the boost interval, the anti-gaming accounting window — and getting the combination wrong for a given workload is easy and hard to detect without careful measurement.

Too few queues and MLFQ can't distinguish behaviors finely enough; too many and the system spends a long time "discovering" where a process belongs before treating it correctly. A boost interval tuned for one workload's typical job length can be badly wrong for a very different one running on the same machine.

This parameter-tuning fragility — not any single flaw — is the main reason Linux moved to CFS's more principled, largely parameter-light fairness model (vruntime comparison) instead of continuing to refine MLFQ's heuristics indefinitely.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in production
slides.markdown:
MLFQ's exact design shaped real, historically significant schedulers: Windows NT's scheduler and the classic Solaris scheduler both use multilevel-feedback-style priority adjustment based on observed CPU usage, and Linux's pre-CFS O(1) scheduler (used from roughly 2.6 through 2.6.22) used similar dynamic priority boosting for interactive processes.

Application-level thread pools and job schedulers borrow the same behavioral-inference idea: a task queue that tracks each job type's historical execution time and routes newly-submitted jobs of that type to a "fast" or "slow" lane based on that history is doing MLFQ's core trick — inferring likely behavior from observed history instead of requiring an upfront promise.

When an interviewer asks "design a scheduler that favors interactive work without starving batch jobs" (a very common system-design-adjacent prompt), MLFQ's rule set — demote on full-quantum use, promote/retain on early yield, periodic full boost — is close to the expected answer shape, even if the final answer references a different concrete mechanism.
